title: Resolution of Infrared Entanglement Divergences via the Extended Uncertainty Principle
abstract: The entanglement entropy of quantum systems typically exhibits both ultraviolet and infrared (IR) divergences. In the low-frequency limit, the IR divergence is intimately tied to the unbounded spatial delocalization of zero-modes, a pathological feature common to both coupled harmonic oscillators and massless scalar fields. In this work, we demonstrate that this infinite growth is naturally resolved by invoking the Extended Uncertainty Principle (EUP), which introduces large-length-scale geometric corrections to the canonical commutation relations. By exactly solving the simple harmonic oscillator under the EUP framework, we establish the existence of an intrinsic geometric confinement that enforces a strict upper bound on the position variance, limits spatial delocalization, and introduces an intrinsic localization length scale related to the background Ricci scalar. We extend this regularizing mechanism to many-body systems by evaluating the entanglement entropy and entanglement spectrum of a one-dimensional harmonic chain and a massless scalar field. We show that the EUP-induced spatial bounds prevent the accumulation of low-lying long-wavelength modes, keeping the entanglement spectrum discrete and evenly gapped even in the strictly massless limit. This non-vanishing modular gap effectively caps the local entanglement temperature of the vacuum. Consequently, the entanglement entropy saturates to a finite value, providing a robust, geometric resolution to the zero-mode IR divergence problem in quantum field theory.
summary: The paper tackles the problem of infrared divergence in entanglement entropy by incorporating the Extended Uncertainty Principle (EUP). By modifying canonical commutation relations, EUP imposes a natural geometric confinement on quantum fields. This confinement successfully regularizes the zero-mode divergences, leading to finite and physically meaningful values for the entanglement entropy.
main_problem: The primary goal is resolving infrared (IR) divergences encountered when calculating entanglement entropy in quantum field theories, which arise from the unbounded delocalization of zero-modes.
main_result: Invoking the Extended Uncertainty Principle (EUP) introduces an intrinsic geometric confinement that bounds spatial variance and causes the entanglement entropy to saturate to a finite value, thus resolving the IR divergence.
method: The authors solve the simple harmonic oscillator under EUP corrections and extend this analysis to many-body systems by calculating entanglement entropy using techniques like moment matching and asymptotic expansion of von Neumann entropy.
model_or_system: The study analyzes quantum systems including simple harmonic oscillators, one-dimensional harmonic chains, and massless scalar fields. The core modification is the EUP applied to canonical commutation relations: [x, p] = i\hbar(1 + \gamma x^2).
key_observables: Entanglement entropy ($S$), entanglement spectrum, spatial variance ($\langle x^2 angle$), and modular gap.
important_parameters:
The EUP parameter $\gamma$ (related to the background Ricci scalar), the frequency $\omega$, and the large-eigenvalue limit $
u \gg 1$.
main_assumptions:
Assumes $\gamma$ is small and finite ($\gamma 
eq 0$) for regularization; relies on asymptotic expansions in various limits.
figures_summary: Figures compare spatial profiles of eigenstates under EUP vs. HUP, and show comparisons of entanglement entropy calculated via RDM versus RCM approaches.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from solving the SHO under EUP to establishing intrinsic confinement, then extends this regularization mechanism to calculate entanglement entropy for harmonic chains and scalar fields in the continuum limit.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, geometric modification (EUP) to address fundamental divergences in quantum field theory observables like entanglement entropy, which is crucial for understanding vacuum structure and correlations in many-body systems.
